 CA Post Editorial Board Updated Thu, November 19, 2026 at 3:09 AM UTC 3 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Students in the UC system are protesting — again. This time, their target is standardized testing , which they claim is racist.
 A few years ago, each of the protesters would have had to take the SAT (which used to stand for the "Scholastic Aptitude Test" but now is simply known by the acronym), and possibly the American College Test (ACT) as part of their application process.
 In 2020, during the moral panic of the Black Lives Matter movement, the University of California regents voted to do away with the SAT and other tests, on the argument that they discriminated against black applicants and certain other "disadvantaged" minorities. 
 Students in the UC system are protesting — again. This time, their target is standardized testing, which they claim is racist. BLAKE FAGAN/EPA/Shutterstock
 A few years ago, each of the protesters would have had to take the SAT (which used to stand for the "Scholastic Aptitude Test" but now is simply known by the acronym), and possibly the American College Test (ACT) as part of their application process. AP
 Doing so likely discriminated against Asian students. But the greater damage was done to the students who were admitted to UC Berkeley and other elite universities on the basis of grades,  essays and recommendations alone.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Many of them simply could not do the work. As The California Post noted , professors at UC Berkeley found that incoming freshmen could not handle basic math like fractions. The world's most brilliant instructors were forced to waste their time on remedial lessons.
 Yes, the student body throughout the UC system was more "diverse." It also was less capable — and students who might have excelled at less demanding schools struggled instead.

 Over 1,000 professors throughout the UC system signed letters this year urging the regents to reconsider.
 Advertisement Advertisement The regents began studying the idea of bringing back standardized testing. This week, for example, they heard from researchers who had studied the relationship between standardized tests and student performance. 
 The experts confirmed that dropping the SAT made schools more diverse. But the regents also heard that low test scores predict poor results at college. And grades alone are not a reliable indicator of preparedness, because schools are so different.
 Many of them simply could not do the work. As The California Post noted, professors at UC Berkeley found that incoming freshmen could not handle basic math like fractions. The world's most brilliant instructors were forced to waste their time on remedial lessons. Newsday via Getty Images
 The problem is not bias in the tests. It's weakness in the schools.
 Outside, as The California Post reported, students held up signs like "Keep the UC Test FREE!" (No points were taken off for a missing hyphen between "test" and "free.")
 Advertisement Advertisement The movement to stop testing has reached high schools, as well, with LAUSD students adding the SAT and ACT to their list of grievances in anti-ICE protests this week.
 Ironically, standardized testing is a lifeline for the best black and Hispanic students — a way for them to signal to universities that they are ready to excel, even if they attended weak schools.
 The UC regents should consider the evidence — and ignore the protests.
